I intervened last evening to suggest at the time the question was initially raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), that there was some doubt as to whether the matter involved a question of privilege. Since that time I have had an opportunity to consider some authorities. I refer Your Honour to the seventeenth edition of May's, page 109, where the following appears:
It may be stated generally that any act or omission which obstructs or impedes either House of Parliament in the performance of its functions, or which obstructs or impedes any member or officer of such House in the discharge of his duty, or which has a tendency, directly or indirectly, to produce such results may be treated as contempt even though there is no precedent of the offence.
The essence of a question of privilege, as I read that citation and citations 102 to 116 in Beauchesne's, is that privilege is a protection for members of the House and is not intended to limit in any way the things members can say in the House. There is a second point I wish to make. Even if a suggestion of this nature has been made, there is a question whether the persons about whom it was made are, in fact, officers of the House, in parliamentary terms. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, with the greatest respect for the
November 13, 1974

good staff which serves us in this place, and for motives about which I can only be suspicious, I think it is stretching things a bit to say that officers of the House, as referred to in the statements yesterday, could ever be implicated. As the right hon. Prime Minister said in his statement today, Your Honour is an officer of the House, just as is the Clerk of the House and the Sergeant-at-Arms.
I think the essence of the matter, first off, is that this is hardly a question of privilege. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised this matter last night in the course of debate, but having examined the authorities I would urge upon Your Honour consideration of those authorities and ask you to rule that this is not a question of privilege for the House, that no member's right is interfered with and that there is nothing here for the Chair to deal with except to turn down this question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF HON. MEMBER FOR NORTHUMBERLAND-DURHAM CONCERNING HOUSE OF COMMONS EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Order, please. I welcome discussion of this subject by hon. members. I have some difficulty with every question of privilege, of course, and this one is no exception. What troubles me about this particular matter is not simply the question of privilege itself. It may, in fact, be possible to decide on the precedents and on the strength of the arguments presented to the Chair that in fact a question of privilege does not exist. Even a prima facie question of privilege may not exist.
However, the problem is more serious than that. The responsibility of the Chair, of course, is the provision of the staff and the supervision and running of the staff that serves the House of Commons. It is the Chair's responsibility to see that the staff performs its functions not only properly but that it is free of any kind of allegation that may be made against it. Therefore, whether or not a prima facie question of privilege exists, the Chair would have the responsibility of seeing, on the basis of an allegation of this sort-if this is the kind of allegation that has been suggested-that the matter be discussed, examined, investigated and reported upon in a very thorough and complete manner.
Accordingly, there seem to me to be two problems here. The first is whether a prima facie question of privilege exists. Then, even if it does not exist, the second and more serious problem is whether the allegations made by the hon. member have any substance to them. Both are very serious and important question and for this reason I was anxious that the hon. member be given the opportunity to clarify the intent of his remarks, so as to determine whether or not there is substance to a specific allegation of any criminal activity in this building.
If there is further discussion to be presented at this time, I propose to reserve my judgment as to whether or not a prima facie question of privilege exists in this matter and inform hon. members of my decision at a later date after further discussion, if such is forthcoming at the moment. In the circumstances, both the House and the Chair might be relieved of this burden if the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham wants to make it perfectly clear, either that he has no specific allegation of criminal activity in this building or, in the alternative, if he does

have a specific allegation of criminal activity, that he is prepared to substantiate it.

But apart altogether from this being a tempest in a teapot, I suggest members of the public are frequently in this building. Not all people who are in this building are members of the public service or agents of Your Honour. I think this should at least seep through the skulls of some people, if they are willing to talk about this subject.
I am merely saying, Mr. Speaker, that if you want to find out where criminal activity exists around here, it is not hard to do so. I say that, sir, on the basis of some friendships that I have made around here with the staff.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOLLOWING VISIT TO PEACEKEEPING UNITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this early opportunity since returning to Canada to report to the House on my trip to visit more than 2,000 members of the Canadian armed forces on peacekeeping duty in Cyprus and in the Middle East.
During the past few days I have been in Cyprus, where there are more than 900 Canadian military personnel; in Egypt, where we have more than 1,000 personnel; in Syria, where we have 29, and in Israel where there are approximately 170. In numerous conversations with members of the Canadian armed forces in these four countries, I found that generally speaking morale is high, and it is clearly evident that our personnel are convinced they are engaged in useful and worthwhile work. They are willing to undergo some of the difficult living conditions and the sacrifice of being separated from their families in order to perform the important task of peacekeeping.
In the United Nations Bolivar camp on the Golan Heights, where living and working conditions are the most difficult, I was encouraged to find that substantial progress is being made in the construction of new buildings and in the improvement of sanitation and living conditions.
Throughout the trip I found that, without exception, the political and military leaders in all four countries praised the work being done by the Canadian contingents of the United Nations forces. I do not want to over-state this matter, but I believe all members of the House would have been as pleased, and as proud, as I was to have heard some of the ways in which our Canadian personnel were described. The adjectives that were most frequently used were, that in carrying out their duties the Canadians are known to be impartial, competent and resourceful.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOLLOWING VISIT TO PEACEKEEPING UNITS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOLLOWING VISIT TO PEACEKEEPING UNITS
speechtext:
In conversations with President Clae-rides and Vice-President Denktash in Cyprus, with the Deputy Premier and Minister of War of Egypt, Field Marshal Ismail, as well as with the Defence Minister of Syria, General Tlass, and the Defence Minister of Israel, Shimon Peres, I was left with no doubt whatsoever that the contribution Canada is making to peacekeeping is welcomed and is well received in each of these countries. There is no doubt at all in my mind that the presence of our forces is helping to provide the stability, and the relatively peaceful conditions, in which meaningful negotiations can take place.
I am pleased to be able to report, specifically, that within the next few days the United Nations will be recommencing flights between Beirut and Damascus, using Canadian Buffalo aircraft. From conversations with the Defence Minister of Syria and his senior officers, I am satisfied that the tragic loss of the United Nations Buffalo aircraft on this route last August was an accident regret-

ted by all, and was not an aggressive act directed against the United Nations.
Last week our own aircraft flew over this same route to Damascus and I have been assured that all future flights of Canadian or United Nations aircraft will travel in safety as far as the Syrians are concerned. The recommencement of Buffalo aircraft flights from Beirut to Damascus will greatly assist in the adequate supply of the Canadian peacekeeping forces now living in the buffer zone on the Golan Heights.
As a result of several on-the-spot conversations which I had with Canadian servicemen, I now intend to examine the feasibility of establishing a Canadian leave centre where personnel serving in Cyprus, or in the Middle East, can spend their leave. Also, whenever appropriate transportation arrangements can be made, it is our hope that servicemen's wives will be able to travel to this leave centre.
One good location for a leave centre would be near the airfield at Akrotiri in the Greek-Cypriot town of Limassol.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express the usual thanks to the minister for having made available at an early point a copy of his statement so that it might be reviewed by us before we make our comments in reply thereto. I appreciate these courtesies which make our work a little easier. Members of the House have just heard, and I trust with some alarm, the amazing statement of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson). One could not help but believe that all is well and rosy within the Canadian armed forces. We welcome the minister's statement to the effect that our forces are doing well and are well received in the Middle East in respect of the two particular assignments with the United Nations. Indeed, there is not a member of this House who does not appreciate the ability of the Canadian forces under such conditions, and their ability to come through very strong and do their job very well.
The minimum statement that was expected by this House, and I think by the Canadian people, had nothing to do with whether or not we are loved over there, but rather with whether or not we are able to fulfil the mandate given us and the responsibility we have over there, or whether or not we will withdraw troops from Cyprus. Why did the minister not bother to tell us more about the progress of negotiations on that torn island so that we might better understand the commitment we are asking ihe Canadian people and the Canadian forces to make in that area. This is what we expected as a minimum. The
Report on Peacekeeping Units
minister mentioned-and there was reference to this in the Canadian Press and the minister referred to it today- that he was there to see whether or not we should pull back troops. We expected him to say today either that he is satisfied with the work being done there and will leave them there or that he will bring some of these forces home.
Why could we not have had a response to questions such as these? These questions concern not only us but also our allies and partners within this joint venture in peacekeeping. It is very meaningful and very serious work. The House is no better informed now than it was the day before the minister went to the Middle East. I am sure we all welcome the fact that he did make this visit. I had hoped that he would have had the courtesy to invite some members from other sectors of this House to make this visit, then we might have had a balanced view and a little bit of hard news about the facts.
There are just one or two other brief comments I should like to make, Mr. Speaker. Our concern, of course, arises out of financing restrictions, lowering force levels, and the fact that it takes five or six men to keep one man in an operational situation. Our concern also is that we do not have the money to logistically support these people and to adequately support rotation. In other words, we cannot perform the multiple tasks assigned in the 1970 White Paper, so it is unrealistic for the minister to stand in this House and make out that all is well. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the armed forces are getting damned sick of the situation. There are very real problems in peacekeeping and we thought that the minister might have dealt with some of them today. We wanted to know what the hopes are for a settlement in these areas but we did not hear anything about that.
I hope that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) might take an early opportunity to meet with the minister and insist on the production of a White Paper which would clearly set out our requirements for national sovereignty, our international responsibilities and the priorities of our peacekeeping role, as well as the multiple taskings that cause difficulties in meeting commitments at home.
With respect to national sovereignty, I hope that the Prime Minister would urge the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) to prepare a statement at the earliest possible moment with respect to the armed forces which would reflect the very desperate situation in which the Canadian armed forces find themselves today.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOLLOWING VISIT TO PEACEKEEPING UNITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do want to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East however, by saying that what we had today was a motherhood statement. It brings very little information to this House about the real problem we are facing in the Middle East. Canada, with justice, has been very proud of the role our peacekeeping forces have played. We are not a major power, not a power with territorial ambition. Our role is very important and is one which this party has supported for a very long time and will continue to support.
I think it is time, however, that we reassessed the peacekeeping role that our forces are playing. The ad hoc financing of Canadian forces is simply not satisfactory. It is time that we had decent backup from the United Nations for our forces.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOLLOWING VISIT TO PEACEKEEPING UNITS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOLLOWING VISIT TO PEACEKEEPING UNITS
speechtext:
It is high time that this government raised this issue in a vigorous manner in the councils of the world and particularly in the United Nations. When our forces are in positions of high risk there is a lack of international support. I can only refer the House to the actions of Gamal Abdal Nasser when our forces were unilaterally ordered out of the Middle East, which action contributed to that war, and the Turkish attitude toward our forces in Cyprus which leaves a lot to be desired and to some extent is disgraceful. We must keep in mind that an attack on Canadian forces in the Middle East is an attack on the United Nations and on the world forces of order. Mr. Speaker, we are just not getting the kind of backup support from the United Nations that we should be getting.
I think we should look again at our basic role, Mr. Speaker, and ask if we are really peacekeepers or merely observers? It is time that we moved to the next stage in peacekeeping, a stage that would give some muscle to peacekeeping. It is time the world imposed sanctions on those nations that see fit to attack peacekeeping forces, and that is the kind of support we must have if the United Nations, indeed the world, is to survive.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOLLOWING VISIT TO PEACEKEEPING UNITS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER FOLLOWING VISIT TO PEACEKEEPING UNITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before making my remarks, I would like to tell the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) that I am unfortunately unable to pay him the same compliments as the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall)

since the French translation of his statement reached us only at 2.35 p.m. I would to point out that we should like to have the French version of his statements at the same time as all other members.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to see that the minister is in great shape after such a hard trip, both physically and morally.
Moreover, I am happy to hear him say that the morale of our soldiers seems very good, but I would rather see them back among us.
Mr. Speaker, we have always provided help for foreign countries and we have also tried to further peace and goodwill through pacific negotiations.
The Canadian participation in the peacekeeping force does not have for its only objective successful negotiations between the conflicting parties. Mr. Speaker, it must ensure that a stable peace is enforced between all the nations of the world.
We shall continue to assert our availability and our wish to serve peace wherever we shall be asked to do so and wherever we may be useful.
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that the wives of our soldiers will be able to visit their husbands. I am certain that this will be very helpful to our Canadian forces.
I would like to note, Mr. Speaker, that a young soldier from my constituency died recently in Cyprus in the defence of peace. It is sad that such things can happen, but the role played by Canada in protecting the peace is essential.
Mr. Speaker, our most sincere desire is that the conflicts between Cyprus and Turkey come to an end as soon as possible.

subtopic: UIC-CRITERIA USED IN DETERMINING DISTANCE WITHIN WHICH AN UNEMPLOYED PERSON CANNOT REFUSE EMPLOYMENT
UIC-CRITERIA USED IN DETERMINING DISTANCE WITHIN WHICH AN UNEMPLOYED PERSON CANNOT REFUSE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
1.	What criteria are used to determine the distance within which an unemployed person, wishing to continue to draw benefit, cannot refuse suitable employment when that person does not possess an automobile and there is no convenient form of public transportation?
2.	Would the same criteria apply to a person whose spouse possesses an automobile?
3.	Does such a judgment on distance vary with the length of unemployment and does it vary by region if all other circumstances are similar?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: UIC-CRITERIA USED IN DETERMINING DISTANCE WITHIN WHICH AN UNEMPLOYED PERSON CANNOT REFUSE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
1. There is no rigid rule to determine the distance beyond which a claimant can refuse suitable employment because of lack of personal transportation or public transportation at convenient times, and remain eligible for benefits. Although distance and transportation facilities are factors considered in determining a claimant's eligibility, they can be offset by other factors such as the normal practice in the area for workers required to commute to and from work daily. Lack of transportation is generally not a good cause in itself for refusing suitable work.
2.	If the claimant could use the spouse's automobile, the commuting distance would then be determined primarily on the distance workers of the area normally travel to work daily.
3.	Neither the length of the period of unemployment nor the geographical location have any bearing on the lack of transportaton factor if the employment offered is suitable. An additional consideration in cases of this nature is that a claimant who has no means of transportation to work generally fails to prove for all practical purposes that he or she is available for work and unable to obtain suitable employment and is not entitled to benefit.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: PROPOSED OFFICERS QUARTERS BRIDGE, RIDEAU CANAL, LEEDS COUNTY
speechtext:
The
Department continues to de-emphasize the use of a brucellosis vaccination for the following reasons: (1) the low incidence of the disease across Canada. (2) the vaccine does not provide immunity in all animals. (3) some vaccinates react to the brucellosis test thus causing confusion in the interpretation of the test due to the fact that it is not possible to distinguish between a vaccination reaction and a reaction from infection. If an owner decides to have his calves vaccinated, the department recommends they be done as soon as possible after three months in order to lessen vaccination reactions on the blood test.

In what proportion of accidents investigated by the Air Accident Investigation Division of the Department of Transport has the investigation or any party thereof been partially or otherwise concerned with any feature, aspect or facet of air transportation in Canada, including certification of air worthiness, pilot licensing, instrument accuracy, flight procedures and pilot notification, that is governed, regulated or in any other way whatsoever directed by any other agency of the Department or any other branch, agency or division of the government?

All accident investigations conducted by the Aviation Accident Investigation Division of the Ministry of Transport are concerned with certification of airworthiness, pilot licensing, instrument accuracy, flight procedures, and pilot notification that are regulated and controlled by the relevant branches and divisions of the Canadian Air Transportation Administration of the Ministry of Transport. However, the accident investigation division does not assess whether or not an infraction of regulations has occurred because the investigators may not be qualified in regulatory matters; they establish causal factors only. The question of the adequacy of regulations and controls is subject to accident investigation scrutiny as are the technical and operational factors, and a significant number of regulations and control procedures have been adopted as a result of findings of accident investigations. In summary, it should be noted that the Ministry of Transport system of air accident investigation is based upon the determination of cause, not blame, and witnesses, be they public servants or private citizens, are offered privilege. The courts have upheld the privilege of the witness statements on two recent occasions. Also there has never been a single instance of litigation against the Crown related to inadequate regulations, or suppression and alteration of accident data, but there have been cases related to improper

subtopic: EXTRACTIVE BASED SHIPPING IN CANADIAN ARCTIC ARCHIPELAGO
speechtext:
As
announced by the Ministry of Transport on September 24, it is intended to implement the recommendations of the Report of the Inquiry on the Coasting Trade of Canada and Related Marine activity, restricting coasting trade activities to Canadian flag vessels. This restriction will include vessels operating in the Arctic Archipelago. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the latest reports showing that medical and health care services in Canada are being crippled by soaring costs, is the federal government now preparing new proposals to put before the provinces to bring these soaring costs under control, and if not, why not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASING COST OF MEDICAL CARE-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS TO PROVINCES TO CONTROL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as was indicated in the hon. member's question, rising costs in the health field corresponds in general to rising costs in the overall economy, resulting from the inflation which we are now experiencing. As for the various methods of financing health care, my colleagues from the provinces should consider some alternatives. I for one am examining whether there is a possibility of developing new methods which would be more appropriate. But, if I may repeat myself, this will take time, and I unfortunately cannot promise the hon. member to give any specific information on that matter before several months.

subtopic: INCREASING COST OF MEDICAL CARE-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS TO PROVINCES TO CONTROL
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Without entering into a debate, the rate of inflation in health services is much greater than the general average. speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASING COST OF MEDICAL CARE-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS TO PROVINCES TO CONTROL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the federal authorities have already made in the past a specific proposal to introduce more flexibility in the financing of health care which would have indirectly led to better control over costs. I have not yet received other provincial proposals. As I indicated in my first answer to the hon. member, I am considering the situation with my officials, but I repeat once again, I will be unable to suggest a formula in the immediate future.

Mr. Chairman, as I understand it, we will have general remarks under clause 2 and later in the debate, hopefully today, we would adjourn clause 2 temporarily and get on with clause 3 so that I can bring forward substantive amendments and have them tabled. My general remarks will be a summary of the objectives we should have in mind.
All members of the House want to produce a good bill. All members of the House want to honour the agreement made by the heads of the 11 governments at the meeting on March 27 this year. All members of the House, I think, have agreed on the principle that we should have a lower oil price all across Canada than the world price. The level below the world price is not stated at this time. There should be however, some form of time formula stated in the bill that will make it clear to industry and to the provinces that this competitive price, to ease the strain on the commercial operations of the various agencies both
November 13, 1974

public and private dealing with oil and gas in Canada, can be made more certain and stable. These two principles, of a lower price and the staging proposal, have to be followed by a third principle, the cushion effect, which I think is adequately dealt with in the bill.
There are other principles I wish to refer to, as I mentioned in the discussion on second reading. I am not satisfied, and I do not think any member would be satisfied, with the fact that there is no mention in the bill, under the "purpose" provision, of a quid pro quo for the provinces. When any government is asked to make a sacrifice in the interest of the national good-in this case, a substantial amount running at the present time from $2!4 billion to $3 billion per year for two provinces-I think it is only fair that we do what we can within that national purpose to make sure there is an indication by this House that, if possible, we will provide a quid pro quo dictated in principle by this House and not through informal discussions between the minister and the producer governments. It will, therefore, be our intention to move at least one, if not two, amendments on the quid pro quo principle, backing that up with a substantive amendment which will give an example of what I mean, so that the House, in effect, directs the type of quid pro quo that it thinks would be fair and equitable.
The final principle on which the main thrust of the debate will centre is the question of consultation. There is no doubt that under the British North America Act the ownership of land and resources resides entirely within the right of the province concerned. There is no question that the federal government has complete sovereign power in interprovincial and export trade. Here we have a situation where the power of one administration acting purely within its constitutional right has the effect, by incidence or by result, of influencing the actions of another legislature, another sovereign power, which in turn is acting purely within its sovereign right. I do not think that in this particular debate the issue at stake is the question of which level of government is the most greedy. What we are trying to do here, as a federal parliament, is to make certain that we bring forward legislation that will not be found unconstitutional and will serve the purpose which we all want it to serve.
I shall give an example of what I mean, Mr. Chairman. For 30 years, during the twenties, thirties and forties, the federal government-formed of both parties which held the reins of power during those years-in good faith used to lease land on Indian reservations to people who were not of Indian extraction; and they used to sell properties, part of Indian reservations, to people off the reservations. The money was turned over to the Indian bands.
This type of action was carried out in almost every province of Canada over many years. The inevitable happened. Although the federal government felt it was acting purely within its constitutional right, namely, that it was responsible for Indian affairs in this country and that it was doing the right thing in leasing land on Indian reservations and selling it with the agreement of the Indians, the moneys going back to the Indians so that it seemed a fair and reasonable activity by the federal government, somebody took the transactions to court. These actions went right up to the Supreme Court and the Privy Coun-
Oil and Petroleum
cil, and it was ruled that when the lands were no longer used for the pure purpose of Indian reservations, they reverted to the Crown, in right of the province. Even though the federal government thought it was acting within its constitutional prerogative in looking after Indian reservations, it found itself in an ultra vires position in respect of these activities vis-a-vis land on Indian reservations.
The government of which I was a member had to face the fact that under the British North America Act, lands in the provinces that were not federal lands and mineral rights in the provinces which did not belong to the federal government, had to be dealt with through the legislatures of the provinces. In other words, we had to obtain the consent of the Crown in right of the provinces. In response to this conclusion, in 1958 the then minister of Indian affairs introduced two bills into this House. One was entitled, "An act to confirm an agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the province of New Brunswick respecting Indian reserves." This particular bill was passed. It has some interesting points. The facts which I have described are set out in the bill. Section 2 of the schedule reads:
All grants of patented lands are hereby confirmed except in so far as such grants purport to transfer to the grantees any minerals and said minerals are hereby acknowledged to be the property of the province.
Even though there was agreement between the province of New Brunswick and the federal government that they would legitimize these particular transactions over the previous 30 years, the federal bill, with the agreement of the province, provided that the province still reserved the right to any minerals in these lands. The mineral rights of these lands which were transferred to the grantees, or to the people who bought or leased them, were kept within the prerogatives of the Crown in right of the province. Section 3 of the schedule reads:
New Brunswick hereby transfers to Canada all rights and interests of the province in reserve lands except lands lying under public highways, and minerals.
I am reading this into the record, Mr. Chairman, to indicate that even though the federal government acted in good faith from 1922 to 1958 and within its constitutional jurisdiction, and felt it could handle problems on Indian reservations across Canada by taking lands out for lease or ownership, it found that it could not move without the consent of the Crown in right of the province. The British North America Act makes it clear, in sections 109 and 125, that minerals are the property of the province and the federal government cannot tax or do anything with them. If any federal action has the effect, through the principle of incidence, of hurting the interests of the other party, in this case New Brunswick, it is ultra vires. Similarly, we must consider the rights of provinces such as Nova Scotia, which provides a similar example.
My point is this: no matter how conscientious and hard working the minister may be, or how sincere his advisers may be, unless the minister can be absolutely certain that he is acting within the constitution we may be heading for trouble. That is why I suggested this method of proceeding, because we can consider these matters and the law officers of the Crown can consider whether, according to

all precedents, what is being done under all clauses is proper. My second point concerns consent. On page 5960 of Hansard of July 14, 1959, the then minister of citizenship and immigration, Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough, is reported to have said the following, in moving second reading of Bill S-6, to confirm an agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the province of New Brunswick respecting Indian reserves:
Mr. Speaker, His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the purpose of this bill, has given consent so far as Her Majesty's property rights are concerned, that the House may do therein as it shall think fit.
The circumstances concerning the prerogative of the Crown in which the bill of 1959 was introduced were similar to those we are now considering. Then the government, since the bill at that time affected the property of the Queen in right of the federal government, obtained consent of the Sovereign. The Sovereign said that the House could do as it saw fit. In other words, the Sovereign did not intend to put obstacles in the way of any decision the House might take at that time. That consent was obtained on the advice of the law officers of the Crown. According to Hansard, the minister went on to say:
The purpose of this legislation is to ratify and confirm an agreement made on March 25, 1958, between the government of Canada and the government of the province of New Brunswick in relation to lands forming part of Indian reserves in the province of New Brunswick. The necessity for such an agreement arose from decisions of the judicial committee of the Privy Council of Great Britain in two cases involving the sale of portions of Indian reserves in Ontario and Quebec, by the federal government, following surrenders for sale given by the Indian bands for whom the reserves had been set apart... In both cases it was held that notwithstanding that Canada had exclusive jurisdiction over lands reserved for Indians, the radical title to the reserves was in the province and therefore, a valid agreement, after a surrender for sale by an Indian band, could only be made by the province.
The spokesman for the official opposition was the then hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi. Apparently he knew a good deal about the matter before the House. He said in part, as recorded at page 5961 of Hansard for July 14, 1959:
Certain cases were appealed to the Privy Council, and it was held that these lands were the property of the Crown in the right of the province. This means that it was necessary to take action to validate the defective grants, and negotiations between the two levels of government have been going on for some ten years and have now ended in mutual agreement.
I am making two points. First, there must be consent by both governments to any dealings affecting the property or prerogatives of the Crown. That is why the minister of that day made the sort of statement which ought to be made now in this House and whenever we are dealing with property or prerogatives of the Crown. Second, once consent to that agreement was obtained, it was ratified by legislation in the provincial legislatures and in parliament which provided the consent of the Crown in right of the province.
Speaking as a layman, I am not at all satisfied that this bill may not be declared beyond the competence of parliament. After all, the British North America Act laid down how the various powers within this country were to be divided. At present I am dealing with the narrow issue of Crown prerogatives. I submit that this bill is unsatisfactory, because the minister has not yet indicated the consent of the Crown in the federal right and there is no evidence

before the committee showing that the Crown in right of the province consents to passage of any parts of the bill which affect the property of the Crown in right of the province. That being so, if I were in the minister's position I would wish to consult the law officers of the Crown before answering. That is why I suggested our present procedure: we can put our views forward, the minister can transmit those views to the law officers of the Crown and receive an answer which we can consider.

The Supreme Court of Canada held that administration of the national oil market, as part of the administration of interprovincial trade, was intra vires of the government of Canada. In this particular case, we are exercising an identical jurisdiction.
In this bill we are exercising jurisdiction by saying that once the particular commodities become products of interprovincial or international commerce, the responsibility clearly given to the federal government under section 91(2) of the British North America Act, for the regulation of trade and commerce, comes into play. At that point it is not only the right, but the responsibility of the federal government to regulate the national market. Provincial measures adopted from time to time, even in total agreement with the object of the government of Canada, cannot in themselves be effective. They could be effectively attacked by either a private party or another province.
Probably the best and most recent evidence that this continues to be a valid exercise of power is the decision taken by the National Energy Board with regard to setting a minimum and maximum export price for gas. At that point, the government of Canada, exercising its powers over international trade, which are no different in this regard from those over interprovincial trade, stipulated the price at which natural gas could be sold in Canada, not only in minimum but in maximum amounts. This stipulation has not been contested by any provincial government nor, as far as I know, by any private party. In this bill we are not expressly or consciously legislating or exercising jurisdiction witb regard to a natural resource of any particular province. We are exercising our jurisdiction over a subject of commerce which has been, or is to be introduced into interprovincial or international trade.
I wish to refer to one other comment made by the hon. member. This issue has been raised from time to time both in debate on this and its predecessor bill. It is the question of quid pro quo. I suppose in every piece of legislation put before parliament it almost inevitably happens that it strikes one part of the country less evenly than another. One need only look at the equalization formula as it applies to certain provinces but not to others. One could look at each of these pieces of legislation and say, "I have to be satisfied that a particular region is getting a quid pro quo or I shall not support this bill."
In this, as in other cases, it is a reasonable observation that exercising this judgment as to what is in the national interest, this parliament should determine whether it is desirable to maintain some restriction on oil and gas prices in Canada for the benefit of consumers in not only this and other provinces, but even in the province of Alberta, in the sense that provincial pricing is accommodated to the interprovincial formula that has been followed. It is in the interest of Canadians generally that the Canadian economy should have the benefit of this price cushion. There should be a protective cushion against the kind of prices imposed upon the western oil consuming nations by the oil producing nations. Therefore, it is not a question of a bargain in this regard; it is a concept of what is in the national interest. I was not a participant at the
Oil and Petroleum
March 27 meeting, but I take it that it was sufficiently in the national interest to motivate the premiers of the producing provinces, as well as the other provinces, to put forward this proposal.
I do not know what the question of a quid pro quo means. I do not know what the quid pro quo is intended to mean in this case. However, I do not think it is desirable for these major pieces of legislation which affect the economy, generally, of Canada to look for a declaration of a quid pro quo in so far as particular interests are concerned.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain has served a useful purpose in raising this matter as a constitutional issue. I do not share some of the views he has expressed, but I think it would be useful to have the minister's department and the law officers look into this matter so we have a clear idea of the position with respect to this legislation.
Far be it from me to pose as a constitutional expert. I am not a lawyer; I have no training in the legal field. Let me deal, first, with the matter of provincial rights. There is no doubt that the minerals, lands and forests within a province are vested in the Queen in right of the provincial government. They have all the responsibility with regard to controlling production and supervising conservation. They also have the right to certain reimbursement when non-renewable resources are exploited within their province. That is why I think it is very important, in establishing any price, that it be kept in mind that the provinces are witnessing the diminution of part of the public domain which cannot be replaced. It is not like a renewable resource such as grain or lumber. When you dispose of a mineral, oil or natural gas, the province is dispossessing itself of a resource. Once taken out, it is gone forever.
It should also be remembered that the royalties which the provincial governments receive from the development of their resources, both renewable and non-renewable, do not represent a clear gain for the provincial treasury. In a great many instances they spend millions of dollars doing surveys, carrying on exploration, mapping, building roads, and so on. If an industrial development follows their exploration, they have the responsibility of providing schools, hospitals and all the other municipal services in the area. Therefore, they are entitled to every consideration when we are talking about exploitation of their basic resources. That is why I was very disturbed when the Minister of Finance suggested in his budget last May that the royalties paid to provincial governments by resource-based industries would not be deductible from income tax. We shall go into that matter when the budget is brought down.
I think anything which appears to be interfering with the rights of a provincial government to develop its resources and reimburse its people for the exploitation of its public domain should be watched very carefully. Even in the matter of setting prices there has to be the maximum amount of consultation with the provinces and, if possible, agreement with the provinces as set out in clauses 22 and 50 which provide for an attempt to enter
1296

November 13, 1974
Oil and Petroleum
into agreement regarding the price to be established. In a federal system such as ours, everything possible should be done by way of consultation rather than by confrontation. This is the goal which should be pursued, and these are the means which ought to be used.
Having said this, I think we should be very clear as to the powers of the federal government. To a layman like myself, it seems there can be no argument at all that the federal government has the legislative or constitutional authority to set prices outside the province in which the goods are produced. I do not think there can be any argument about its authority to fix the price once the commodity crosses a provincial or international boundary. From my reading of this bill, that is perfectly clear. Clause 20 provides:
This part applies to crude oil which enters into international or interprovincial trade or that is mixed or blended with crude oil which has been acquired for movement out of its province of production.
Clause 24, setting out particulars, provides:
No person shall
(a)	sell any quality or kind of crude oil for consumption outside its
province of production,
(b)	purchase any quality or kind of crude oil for consumption
outside its province of production
Subsequent paragraphs use precisely the same wording. Later, we come to clause 27 which reads:
Every person who acquires any crude oil in a province other than its province of production shall keep records and books of account at its place of business in Canada, or elsewhere in Canada-
We shall, of course, be glad to hear the comments of the minister, the opinions of the law officers and arguments of hon. members generally on this point. However, it seems to me, on the face of it, that the powers which are sought in this legislation are within the authority of the federal government. As a matter of fact, I do not know how selective price controls could be possible unless there were federal jurisdiction over goods moving into interprovincial or international trade. I do not know how there could be a two-price system for oil unless the federal government had such power.
If Canadians are to be cushioned against outrageously high international prices for oil by policies enabling them to buy their supplies at a price lower than the world price, while at the same time permitting our oil to be exported at the world price, with the governments of Canada, federal and provincial, picking up the difference between the two prices, I do not know how all this could be done unless the federal government had the kind of authority contained in the legislation before us.
The provincial governments, certainly the people I have talked to in the producing provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, recognize the logic of that position. The question they raise is the one to which the minister himself referred a few minutes ago. They ask, "What is the quid pro quo?" They say, "You are not doing this with regard to steel, cement, automobiles or machinery. You are doing nothing about freight rates which have militated for decades against western Canada and the Atlantic provinces." This argument is a valid one, in my opinion. The minister cannot very well comment on it now, but I think he should tell his colleagues that the lack of anything which can be regarded as a quid pro quo sticks

in the throats of people in the producing provinces who say, "Whenever we have something the rest of the country needs, there is a price control imposed as soon as it crosses provincial boundaries. But whenever we buy farm machinery, cement, trucks, automobiles and a host of other commodities which enter into our cost of production, we are obliged to pay the going price."
I believe the federal government has the right, constitutionally, to the. power it is seeking in this legislation. I hope it will not be used unwisely. I should like to ask the minister, for instance, what reaction he has received from the oil and gas producing provinces to the proposals contained in this bill and the list of amendments which he courteously sent over to us. Are those provinces prepared to co-operate? What are the possibilities of getting a voluntary agreement on the price of oil under clause 22 rather than having to use the mandatory clause 36? What are the possibilities, as a result of discussion, of getting a voluntary agreement on the price of natural gas as provided for in clause 50 rather than having to use the mandatory provision in clause 52? I am not objecting to clauses 36 and 52. We shall be dealing with those clauses when we come to them.
I do not think any federal government responsible for governing the nation could carry on negotiations indefinitely as to the price of oil and gas while the public continued in a state of uncertainty. I think there comes a time when somebody must have the authority to say, "This is what the price will be." Nevertheless, I ask the minister what reaction he has received from the provinces respecting voluntary agreement. There is another question I want to ask. I think the answer to it might make a considerable difference to the attitude of the oil producing provinces. What does the federal government propose to do with any money in the export charge fund that is left over after these compensation cost payments have been made? The estimate last year was that the government would probably take in $1,300 million or $1,400 million. It was estimated they might pay out in compensation costs, in the area east of the Ottawa Valley, $800 million or $900 million. I asked the minister in the national resources committee what the government was proposing to do with any money that was left over, and he quite properly said that we should wait and see whether there was any money left over. That is why he would not allocate money he had not received.
I should like to know whether any money will be left over, and whether any of it will go to the oil producing provinces. Originally, when the minister made the proposal about divvying up the money from oil, the provinces were going to get 50 per cent of the export tax revenue. Now, in lieu of getting a slightly higher price for the oil, the provinces have no claim on any part of the revenue from the export charge. If several hundred million dollars are left in the fund after compensation payments have been made, then I think the provinces will feel that at least part of the money, if not all, ought to go back to them.
I think the people in the oil producing provinces are good Canadians and are prepared to say that all the money necessary should be taken out of the export charge fund to
November 13, 1974

compensate the people of eastern Canada so that they pay the same price for their oil, plus whatever transportation and handling charges there are, as other Canadians. But I think they would feel very much upset if $400 million or $500 million were left in the fund and the federal government said, "By virtue of the power that we have under the Petroleum Administration Act, we intend to take this money into general revenue". I think that would only exacerbate any feelings of resentment that there are.
I close by saying that I think, as every member here knows, that a federal system creates many problems which you do not have in a unitary form of government. It has advantages in that it makes for better decentralization and for government closer to the people. But it has the disadvantage that we are always concerned about conflicting interests between provincial and federal authorities. Anything that can be done to militate against these feelings of hostility, and to convince people that one part of Canada is not being treated differently from another part, ought to be done.
I think one of the ways of doing this is for the minister and the government to give very serious consideration to stating that if there are funds collected from oil that is exported which are in excess of the money we have to pay to compensate the people of eastern Canada, then either all this money, or certainly a substantial part of it ought to go to the oil producing provinces. If the minister can give us any information on the two or three points that I have raised, I would certainly appreciate it.

Mb. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain): I am very grateful to the hon. member for Calgary Centre for letting me go back to that point at this moment. My remarks are in reply to what the minister has said in outlining the future position on a constitutional basis. May I say at this time that I agree 100 per cent with everything the minister has said, as did the hon. member who spoke for the NDP. However, he has not met the point I was trying to put forward. I would accept the suggestion

that I did not express it very clearly, because it is a very difficult point.
What I am trying to say is that property of a province in the form of land is not just subject to the legislative prerogative of that province but also to the prerogative of the Crown, and if anything happens through the principle of incidence to affect the prerogative of the Crown, then this legislation will become dubious if it goes before the courts. For example, the federal government has legislative authority to control production, whether it be of oil or gas, crossing a provincial border; but the application of that restraint on price, or control of price, has an incidence on the value of the property.
For example, if there were a surplus of $200 million, in this calendar year, of money collected by the federal government in export tax-which the federal government has the power to impose and collect-over the amount paid in compensation under this bill-and the federal government has the power to provide that compensation-I would ask, as a layman, who would own this money if the matter was brought before the courts? This is a depleting resource of the province, and in theory the property, the land or the resource is subject to the Queen's prerogative and can only be altered with the consent of the Queen in right of the province, which means its executive or the legislature. If the minister accepts the seriousness of my case, it would seem that neither he nor I can answer that question. Therefore, the amendments we shall put forward are intended to prevent this type of situation occurring. If the matter went to the courts, it would throw out the whole system which by mutual agreement we are all trying to put into this area.
Therefore, I come back to the key point raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, namely, that the way to avoid all these risks and the potential danger of court action is by agreement mutually arrived at. With such a safeguard in this legislation we would protect the ownership and the rights of the federal government in this field. I would think, therefore, that the debate has come to the crunch. We are not debating the legislative competence of the federal government in fields of interprovincial and international trade, nor are we debating the fact that the provinces own these resources; but what I am putting to the minister as a question that should be of as much concern to him as it is to all of us is, what are the law officers going to say on the question of the Queen's prerogative in respect of the ownership of these resources by the people of Saskatchewan and Alberta?
I put that question to the minister because I do not know the answer. I suggest that very few of us here have an answer, but with all the precedents this matter is worthy of very serious consideration. That is why I mentioned the case of the Indian lands, because after 25 or 30 years of doing something, to finally realize one has made a big, fat boo-boo does not mean we should repeat the same mistake. That is the message I am trying to get across to the minister in a constructive way, to see if we cannot produce better legislation.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands spent most of his life on the prairies. I am sure he shares with me the knowledge that the wealth of the people on the prairies, relative to the people in Ontario and Quebec,
November 13, 1974

is pretty good; but that does not resolve their difficulties. They know, as surely as they exist, that they are part of a colonial structure and even though the four western provinces produce 70 per cent of the wealth of this nation, they represent only 20 per cent or 25 per cent of our population and the representation in this House. They still get this treatment from the central provinces, even though they produce 70 per cent of the basic wealth, and there will be even more coming from our provinces. They have no say in the running of this country and no share in the national interest. We must do something to cushion the shock of the rapidly accelerating price of oil and asking that the producing provinces bear this subsidy of $2,500 million to $3,000 million out of their depleting resources.
The westerner keeps asking himself when he will see signs of equal status among all the provinces. Are they not all equal? Are they not all equal, not only in respect of what they receive from confederation but in respect of their responsibilities? The question I asked of the Prime Minister in respect of electricity was along the same line. Here we have one province endangering another province. I think it is potentially dangerous in the province of Ontario to have one of its plants out of operation, to have another damaged through fire, and to have a coal strike in the United States. Although this situation may not be dangerous, it could be dangerous. Ontario is still our largest industrial complex.
We all ask ourselves, on this issue, not what is right but, rather, what seems to be right; that is, when will this government apply the principle of equality on this very vital energy source, electricity, and ask the province of Quebec to consider its responsibility to the whole country and not be busily negotiating the sale of its surplus power to the United States when a neighbouring part of the Dominion of Canada needs that power.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands mentioned many other things. We think, in this House, traditionally of our transportation difficulties. What about lumber in the province of British Columbia? Last year, when the prairie provinces and Ontario were short, there was no action by this government to bring about equality of sacrifice. When it affects the prairies, do we get called upon to make the supreme sacrifice! I am simply pointing out, on the political issue, that perhaps this bill should be visualized by the minister as more than an administrative-legislative act to carry out the agreement of the eleven governments. As part of a policy of his government, I think he should recognize there is a political fact at stake, and he should put into the bill clauses which will guarantee reasonable equity to the provinces which are under the gun-in this case Alberta and Saskatchewan.
I speak with some feeling because this bill has political connotations. Westerners are waiting to see when the government will treat them as equals. I want to show the House this book by Dr. Ollivier, who once sat at the table where you are sitting now, Mr. Chairman. It has reference to the British North America Act and selected statutes. The preamble refers to the Saskatchewan Natural Resources Act and the Alberta Natural Resources Act of 1930. Mr. Chairman, if I might refer again to the question which the hon. member raised, I do not know whether I followed his argument exactly, but it seems to me the essence of it is that the Crown in right of a province could, by exercising its right in respect of a particular commodity, thereby oust all the legislative jurisdiction of the government of Canada. If that was the question put to me, I think the answer clearly would be no. Clearly, the powers of the government of Canada given under section 91(2) would, for example in interprovincial trade, as much affect the property rights of a province as a private individual. Surely this has to be the structure of the whole statute, otherwise there would have been no basis for the division of power in the first place.
The hon. gentleman referred to a question he posed to the Prime Minister during my absence yesterday in Calgary, with regard to the possible power interconnection between Ontario and Quebec. The first comment I would make is that there is already such an interconnection. Following the January energy conference, I wrote to all the premiers indicating our interest in establishing closer interregional connection, given the unfeasibility at the moment of the kind of national connection which is sometimes talked about in the press. I received answers from the provinces.
In particular, both Ontario and Quebec have indicated approval in principle of the concept of regional interconnection, but both laid very considerable stress on the point that they would take the lead themselves, as provinces, in negotiating those types of arrangements and, if I may say so, in a rather polite way they indicated they would not thank the federal government for telling them the kind of interconnection they should have in this regard. As to the question of an emergency export of power from Quebec, of course under the terms of the National Energy Board Act the applicant, Hydro-Quebec in this case, would have to satisfy the National Energy Board that there was a surplus available in excess of that which would meet the reason-

So the jurisdiction is already there and is established under the National Energy Board Act-indeed it is exercised by the National Energy Board-to make certain that if there are problems for Ontario Hydro this winter, and if it has difficulty and does not seem to be rushing for federal assistance in this regard, before a neighbouring province could export power which could assist it, that province would have to seek the concurrence of the National Energy Board, and the National Energy Board would have to be satisfied in that regard.

speechtext:
The marketplace was restricted, just as it has been restricted for automobiles and other things in the past, by tariffs. There is nothing new in restricting the marketplace. I think it is a rather

generous extrapolation, however, to suggest that something like a tariff or a restriction of imports is tantamount to price control. It simply is not.
I am disappointed, Mr. Chairman, that the minister's reaction to the quid pro quo situation is that this is not in the national interest. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands asked, why is it not in the national interest to be concerned about the legitimate aspirations of western Canadians? Why must a problem be located in central Canada before it is a national problem, and problems elsewhere are regional problems? This attitude is at the root of many of the difficulties we are facing today. This psychological hang-up must be surmounted if we are ever to have a sense of unity in this country.
Originally, all the funds were to go to the producing provinces. Then a 50-50 split was agreed upon, with the provinces also to get the increase in the price of crude from $4 to $6.50 a barrel. The budget came out and confiscated that, but today the minister says it will be considered. I would have to see it in writing, Mr. Chairman, before I could put any trust in it. There are four cases of revenue-sharing where a commitment was made and then immediately broken.
On the matter of rights and constitutional prerogatives, there is no question that the federal government has jurisdiction over trade and commerce, and the provinces own the natural resources. But it seems to me there is also no question that there is no such thing as an absolute right, any more than the right of freedom of speech or freedom of the press allows slander or libel, any more than the freedom of religion allows one to make human sacrifice at some temple. A right is a right only to the extent that it does not impinge upon the rights of others. It is not good enough to say that because the federal government has jurisdiction over trade and commerce, they can effectively do away with any of the normal rights associated with ownership. What does ownership mean, if it entails a denial of the right to dispose of property, if it is dictated where the property shall be disposed of and at what price? Such conditions make ownership meaningless.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands indicated that there may be some necessity for clause 36, the veto clause which would allow the federal government to impose its will unilaterally in the case that no agreement was reached on price. It is my contention, Mr. Chairman, that this clause should be eliminated for a number of reasons. Aside from the question of whether there are constitutional powers to enact that clause, it is a slap in the face for the producing provinces. It is tantamount to suggesting that we do not have confidence in their magnanimity, that we do not trust them to act as loyal Canadians. I do not believe that is a proper attitude for the federal government to adopt.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain referred to the numerous, long-standing grievances of the producing provinces which have been presented to the government but apparently have fallen on deaf ears. The present situation in terms of oil, gas and energy gives the west some leverage, for the first time in 100 years, through which it can demand adjustments in the policies that have worked against it for so long. If we were now to step aside,
November 13, 1974

to deny that leverage to the western provinces, it might be another 100 years before they would be in that position again.
There are other and more important reasons why the government should seriously consider removing this clause. Under the British North America Act, provincial legislatures are not without muscle. It does not take much imagination to see that several pieces of legislative artillery could be introduced by the provinces to counteract any aspect of this legislation felt to be detrimental to their interests. The federal-provincial fight has been escalating for a year and a half. In my own province it has resulted in a lot of genuine people seriously considering the future as a separate political entity. This is of tremendous concern to myself and the majority of Albertans who are Canadians first and foremost. But it is understandable, Mr. Chairman, and anybody with a little sensitivity can appreciate why some people have arrived at that point of view.
Clause 36 was not part of the agreement reached by the first ministers on March 27, yet the federal government, in effect, is saying they are going to continue the fight because under the British North America Act they think they can win it. If they continue with that attitude, there will be very serious consequences for this country which I hope we all love. But I think the country has had enough of this bickering, Mr. Chairman. It is time we came together and talked about consulting and working together, instead of fighting.
The first, important step the federal government should take is saying, "We have confidence in co-operative federalism and in the federal state. We have confidence in provincial premiers who are concerned for the rest of Canada. We believe we can work out our difficulties next July, in the same way as they were worked out last March." That advice does not come from me alone, nor from members on this side alone; it is expressed in a document which the Minister of Energy Mines and Resources tabled in July, 1973, entitled "An Energy Policy for Canada, Phase 1." For example, on page 9 one finds the following:
Federal and provincial responsibilities and interests in the energy field are intimately interrelated. No national policy can be contemplated without the fullest of intergovernmental consultations and consensus.
On page 58 one reads the following:
While the federal government considers that it is its responsibility to take the lead in the development of national energy policies, it recognizes that, generally speaking, these should evolve from the harmonization of the priorities and policies of the several provinces and of the different regional concerns.
That is excellent advice. Lower on the same page one reads the following:
That there can be no effective set of national energy policies developed without the participation of the provincial governments is readily apparent. The provinces own 90 per cent of the assets of the electricity generating industry in Canada, they control almost 100 per cent of the oil and gas produced in Canada today, and, when the potential of the oil sands is included, they control a majority of Canada's future petroleum potential. They also hold the rights to almost all of the coal potential which will meet future energy needs. Obviously, policies developed in isolation in Ottawa hold scant hope for success.
Oil and Petroleum
That is precisely true. That is excellent advice prepared by the minister's department. I wish it were followed. Some may consider this a debate on provincial rights. It is not. The provinces can look after their own rights. They can muster all the legal and legislative muscle which is necessary to take care of their rights-of that you can be sure. The point is that we, as federal members of parliament who are concerned about the entire country, cannot stand aside and allow the escalation which has been continuing for the last year and a half to carry on. We have witnessed what looks like empire building on the part of conflicting bureaucracies who say, "The people of Canada be damned." That attitude is neither acceptable nor responsible.
I shall not touch upon federal and provincial jurisdiction, preferring to deal with that matter when we deal with the appropriate clauses. The bill says nothing about supply, which is regrettable. It talks about protecting consumers from unstable prices. Indeed, it is becoming ever more apparent that we need to guarantee stability of supply; we should not worry so much about price. Unless current trends are reversed, oil and gas will not be available no matter how much we are willing to pay.
I am disturbed because the bill sets no time limit for government controls. Are permanent price controls to be introduced? The minister said this is not the case and implied that this is to be a temporary regime. I agree that no one can see into the future and we do not know what will happen. Nonetheless, introducing such controls, without saying for how long they are to last, is setting a dangerous precedent which may lead to permanent price controls. If the imposition of such controls is in line with the conscious wish of parliament, then for goodness sake let us talk about it publicly. Let there be legitimate, public debate on the question and let us not sneak into a system of controls by the back door. Also, I am not satisfied with the way in which the bill deals with natural gas. Clearly, this matter has not been considered carefully enough. The government has open to it many alternatives for dealing with natural gas. Again, past actions smack more of empire building than of any legitimate response to meet a difficulty.
The subsidy program, on which I commented previoulsy, is the most complicated one can imagine. It purports to take into account every boatload of oil which arrives in this country and, on the basis of a complicated formula, to determine the subsidy which will apply to that oil. Why is a single export tax levied on every barrel of oil produced in this country, regardless of quality, place of production, specific gravity or destination? Why is it necessary to apply a complicated formula to imported oil, a formula which is difficult to administer and which has resulted, despite the government's commitment to a uniform price system across Canada, in crude oil in Montreal being less expensive than crude oil in Toronto? The subsidy program has brought this result: crude oil in the Quebec market is cheaper than crude oil in the Ontario market. That runs counter to supposed government policy. These remarks show some of the weaknesses of the bill.
Whether we are locked into our positions, and whether it is impossible or too late for change, I do not know. I hope it is not too late. I hope, if the government is con-

cerned about the unity of this country, that it will reconsider the necessity for clause 36 of the bill and withdraw it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to speak on Bill C-32.1 do so because of certain statements made a short while ago by the minister in response to certain questions. Having looked at the bill, I realize that it confers tremendous powers upon the federal government. As a colleague of mine suggests, they are enough to make your hair stand on end. The bill deals with gas. According to clause 2-
'gas' means natural gas or any fluid hydrocarbon or any fluid mixture of hydrocarbons other than a hydrocarbon recovered in liquid or solid state-
And so on. Contrary to the minister's statement a short while ago, I understand that the Newfoundland government will not accept a purely advisory role in the management of our east coast offshore resources. In fact, consultations held to date on the amendment question have resulted in a provincial advisory role, this being all that the federal government will concede. The minister, in his reply, can explain to the House why this is so.
I would point out that as a result of this adamant stand, Newfoundland has, in its determination to seek solid provincial management rights, been forced to take independent action in order to secure greater control over its offshore resources. Unfortunately, the other Atlantic provinces do not seem as determined as the government of Newfoundland to obtain this form of management and control. This is regrettable in light of the discovery off the coast of Nova Scotia, for example, on Sable Island. It is unfortunate for the province of Nova Scotia and its future.
The minister now knows the government of Newfoundland will not easily retreat from its present stand. In fact, if negotiations with the federal government fail, it is my understanding the Newfoundland government will take this issue to the Supreme Court of Canada. This is not just a matter of dollars and cents. The first decisions in this federal-provincial dispute relate to the granting of exploration and production permits in the offshore areas. What level of government will be responsible for issuing them? The exploration and production permits will determine the terms and conditions under which the oil companies will participate in the offshore development. Under this bill, who will have final authority in this matter?
Second, Newfoundland wants a strong voice in determining the type of field practices which will be carried out by the oil companies. This is very important, because it will cover such items as conservation and the rate of production. The type of field practices carried out is also a very important question in view of the area in which exploration and development will be carried out, mainly

on our offshore banks where our fish stocks are spawned and where oil pollution presents a further threat to our fish resources.
I can well understand the concern expressed by the government of Newfoundland over this matter. They, like those of us who reside in Nova Scotia, realize our lack of surveillance capability in Atlantic Canada. It is in such a difficult position as to be almost absurd. This is a very valid concern that is being expressed by the government of Newfoundland, because they realize that without surveillance just about anything can happen and is happening on our offshore banks.
Finally, the government of Newfoundland believes it must have a say in determining how any resource products are marketed and used, once they are established. In these three areas the Newfoundland government has refused to accept only an advisory role. It is only fair and proper that the minister explain to this House just what the position will be, not only for the government of Newfoundland but for the other Atlantic provinces, because this is an ongoing dispute; it has not been resolved although discoveries have been made which are worth while.
In my opinion, the federal-provincial relationship should be more of a partnership than having Ottawa end up with ultimate control of these resources. I am not a constitutional expert, but it is my understanding that under the British North America Act the resources of this country belong to the provinces. By giving the federal government final control, I believe we are playing fast and loose with the constitutional balances in this country. There is no reason why our offshore resources should be treated any differently from resources found on land. I believe our provincial governments, especially those in Atlantic Canada, should back up that concept with all the force at their command. I say this because within a few years our oil and gas resources in Atlantic Canada may well be making a meaningful contribution to our energy needs not only in Atlantic Canada but throughout the eastern part of this country. The discovery of natural gas off Labrador in two areas, for example, is very meaningful. Although it is too early to evaluate the commercial potential of these two finds, they are, hopefully, the forerunners of more discoveries in this area.
In conclusion, the absence of a federal-provincial agreement on our offshore areas has unfortunately acted as a negative factor in our attempts to spur additional exploration activity. In fact, federal proposals for heavily taxing our resource companies could have a serious and damaging effect on our rate of exploration and development activities. I have raised some very important points. I have spoken about the concerns of the premiers in Atlantic Canada, primarily Newfoundland. In his reply I hope the minister will not only answer these points but will give us a little better understanding of his concept of the British North America Act and of provincial and federal rights as he sees them under the act.

Mr. Chairman, I should make it clear to the hon. member that this proposed bill does not deal with the question of exploration for and development of oil and natural gas, either in any province or offshore, or federal territory. It deals with oil and gas
