marketing after the product is produced and once the intention is fixed to move it to interprovincial or international trade. In that sense, the question of negotiations with the eastern provinces and the kind of regime which will apply there are relevant and important in another context. They were the subject matter of discussion with Newfoundland, for example, by myself as recently as last week. However, the Petroleum Administration Act does not deal with that question. From the standpoint of the Atlantic provinces, it provides the means and assures that consumers of oil and oil products in the hon. member's province, the other three Atlantic provinces, as well as Quebec and eastern Ontario, will not have to pay international market prices for the products they use.
The policy of the federal government is to have this cushion which has been much objected to by some producing provinces. By this cushion we have taken action to protect the hon. member's province and other provinces from the full impact of international prices. The question he raises is very important, but in another context and in another bill. There is nothing in this bill dealing with either administration of offshore resources or, indeed, exploration and production in any province, at this point.

speechtext: Can the minister explain how gas is developed in Atlantic Canada, specifically off the coast of Labrador, to the point of selling it to Quebec, for example? Will the minister explain how this can be done by the government of Newfoundland? In other words, am I correct in interpreting the minister's comments in this way, that it will be quite acceptable for the government of Newfoundland to establish its own marketing agency for gas they discover off Labrador and to sell this gas to the people of la belle province, Newfoundland or Nova Scotia without running afoul, as we say in the maritimes, of the minister's regulations? Is this a correct interpretation?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE ADMINISTRATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL, EXPORT AND IMPORT TRADE IN PETROLEUM AND PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. This government does not concede that the continental shelf is within the jurisdiction of the government of Newfoundland. That is really what the discussion is all about. In any event, if the gas finds were within the inland waters of a particular province, exploration and production there might well be within provincial jurisdiction. However, once the commodity was introduced into interprovincial or international commerce, the federal jurisdiction over trade and commerce would operate and this bill would apply to it.

I am surprised to hear that expression of surprise from the hon. gentleman, since this has been the issue for the last seven years or more. In the case of the hon. member's own province, the question was taken to the Supreme Court and it was held that the areas beyond low-water mark, with the exception of the inland waters as defined at the time of confederation, were within the jurisdiction of the government of Canada. It happens that in the hon. member's province the provincial government is more interested in preventing exploration and development of hydrocarbons than in making it possible, but that is another question altogether.
With regard to Hudson Bay, I think it is clear that beyond the low-water mark, in the grants by which the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba were given jurisdiction, was withheld from the grant and remains in the federal sector as, indeed, it does in the north.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill raises important questions of principle. First, it pits one region of Canada, the west, against the central market. In effect, it tells western producers that they must sell the goods they produce at a great deal less than their value. This leads us to examine the whole concept of provincial rights. In practice, the provinces are being asked to give up control over their products except that in the case of oil and gas they perhaps have a choice whether to leave them in the ground.
In the second place, the bill sets a price of $6.50 a barrel for oil without saying what is to happen in the future. Most people think the price of oil is bound to reach the world price eventually, but there is no indication here of the means by which increases in price will be permitted. At the purchase level it does nothing for conservation. By setting a lower price, consumption is encouraged. All of us recognize the need of a person to keep warm, but what about the man who drives a large car or who uses a 90 horse-power motor on his power boat when he wants to water-ski? Is he entitled to the same consumer benefits as, say, a pensioner?
The arrangements contemplated in this bill will displace the market as a means of setting the price of gas and oil. With the market no longer functioning, one has to rely on the political process, which means that one or two people with a special interest will set the price. Eventually, the whole country will suffer. In Canada, with its immense distances, market forces should prevail whenever possible or reasonable. Oil and gas are no exception. The prairie governments are very sensitive to attacks on their oil and gas interests. In fact, they are as jealous of those interests as the people of Quebec are about their language.
The struggle of the western provinces to get their natural resources back from Ottawa was long and bitter. It lasted from 1900 to 1929. Now the federal government is attempting to take those rights back again. Mr. J. W. Defoe, editor of the Winnipeg Free Press and one of the staunchest Liberals in history, did a great deal for the Liberal party in western Canada and much to keep this issue alive. We now have a Liberal government in Ottawa backtracking again. When the western provinces were first formed, Ottawa until 1935 treated them as if they were quite incapable of managing their own resources, even though section 109 of the British North America Act provides as follows:
All lands, mines, minerals, and royalties belonging to the several provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick at the Union, and all sums then due and payable for such lands, mines, minerals, or royalties, shall belong to the several provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick in which the same are situate or arise-
The use of revenue from resource development was accepted in principle, but when Manitoba tried to be

treated like the other provinces, Ottawa refused. When the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta came into existence in 1905 they made a similar request and were also refused. This shows how seriously the western provinces regard this as an attack on the resources they own. The feeling was so great that the Conservative Party of 1911 had as one of its pledges that the western provinces would be put on the same footing as other provinces. Nothing came of this until in the 1920s the western progressives supported the Liberals and used this as a lever on the Liberal party to give the western provinces their resources. The government of the day bought off the maritimers with some sweeteners, since the maritimers said that they were entitled to some of the resources in the western provinces.
The federal government of that day sold a great deal of land, some 200 million acres, comprising school land, and so on, and there followed a long and bitter hassle over the amount of compensation to be paid. Alberta claimed for the coal, oil and gas that had been produced up till 1930, and to show that the federal government of that day was not interested in conservation-or perhaps, to be fair, did not take into account conservation-they drew the oil and gas leases in the Turner Valley and billions of cubic feet of gas were wasted. It took a special act of parliament to enable Alberta to enact natural resource conservation legislation.
Some people contend that the federal government is the only body with an over-all view of this country. They say it is the only body capable of marrying up conservation, production of oil and usage. Here we have an example of a provincial government having to step in to conserve a valuable reserve of natural gas. Ultimately, a royal commission awarded the two provinces $5 million, but by this time they were so heavily in debt owing to unemployment that this was a sort of saw-off.
It is very important to the western provinces that jurisdiction over natural resources remain within the province, even in times of emergency such as the present, if I may call it that. If there are emergencies arising because of price, we should not lose sight of the very important fact that the western provinces in particular, though I think all parts of Canada, will function better, nationally, if they remain in control of their resources. For example, we were told that the price of copper in Canada is lower than the world price, that we have a two-price system, but that Ontario is the main loser. Nevertheless, the province of Ontario must stand to gain something, with their large industrial base.
All the good things that have come to the west in recent years have been due to the wealth of natural resources. Saskatchewan has its potash as well as its oil fields, and these resources have made for a better economy. Manitoba has its hydroelectric development, which is still in course of completion and will be very valuable to the province. If this bill fails to recognize the right of the provinces to control their own resources, then I think unity in Canada is in for a very rough ride. The west has fought a long time, as I have detailed, to get possession of its resources and to keep them so as to preserve unto itself some clout in the Canadien confederation. If the federal government takes over the resources of the provinces through the
November 13, 1974

instrument of this bill, then the provinces themselves will move into the field.
It has been suggested by the Hon. Eric Kierans that the provincial governments would probably take over all exploration and development of Canada's resources within a period of five to ten years. Perhaps they will, and perhaps they won't; but from the tax point of view alone, the provincial governments are almost obligated to move into the field. For example, taxes on utility companies and hydroelectric companies are such that Crown corporations are at a distinct advantage. The provincial governments almost have to take over public utilities in order to stop the federal government getting too much revenue. If the provinces do move in-and they may have to-then they could do so in different ways. One way would be to do almost what the Arabs are doing in the Middle East, which is allowing companies only a few cents a barrel to pump out the oil and to claim a heavy tax. But no matter what method is used, it will not likely make for any cheaper oil and gas in the rest of the country.
I, for one, believe that the private sector has a large part to play in the oil and gas industry. I feel that letting the provinces manage and control this industry is much the best way of extracting these resources from the ground. I see little point in the provinces themselves having to take over production of the resources. I think people in general would sooner deal with private companies for their supplies of oil, gas and hydroelectric power, assuming the price is reasonable, than deal with a Crown corporation.
Now, what about the consumer? The bill seems to indicate that it is in the interests of consumers to have relatively cheap energy all across the country. I suggest that if everything were the same price across the country we would find ourselves in an impossible situation. A bill setting the price at $6.50 a barrel, giving no indication as to when the price rise will occur or how it will come about, flies in the face of any practical reasoning. If we are to have a lower price than the world market price, let us have some priority as to those who should benefit from the lower price.
Canada is one of the few nations of the world which increased its energy commitments and capacity in the last year. Even United States commitments and capacity have remained almost steady. The days of cheap energy are all but over. Let me quote what former energy chief John Sawhill of the United States said, as reported in the Toronto Star of November 12, 1974;
I think ... the time is coming when we've got to be honest with the American people and tell them the prices of energy are going to be higher in the future than in the past.
This bill seems to indicate that we will continue to have an everlasting supply of oil at prices lower than world market prices, and that we will continue to take a "head in the sand" attitude. I suggest that because of this attitude Canada is still without a rational, all-embracing energy policy. This bill indicates to Canadians that they can go on blithely convinced that we are wallowing in energy resources. That is not the case. We have lots of energy, but it is very expensive to produce or extract. For instance, it costs in the neighbourhood of $1 billion per year per plant
Oil and Petroleum
to extract petroleum from the tar sands. On the basis of that cost we are looking at oil in the neighbourhood of $10 to $12 per barrel.
This bill sets a price of $6.50 per barrel on oil whether it is old, new, or whatever. There may be a good argument for suggesting that old oil produced in the past and based on a lower tax structure should be put into the pot at a much lower level than new oil. However, at a time when we know that the United States is operating on the basis of $10 a barrel, and at a time when our drilling rigs are moving to foreign areas, we are allowing the same $6.50 a barrel for oil produced in a tar sands plant and for oil produced from wells no matter at what depth.
This bill does nothing to encourage the development of new supplies, and that will be important. Unless this bill shows a greater awareness of that need, we are faced with a difficult future. We are in for a rude awakening very soon because we will not have enough oil, and what we do have will be at a much higher price. Unfortunately, it is hard for people to face up to the dilemma with which we are faced. We all agree that conservation is good, but none of us really wants to practice conservation measures. This bill sets the oil price at $6.50 a barrel, with no indication as to how that figure will change. To all intents and purposes, the bill perpetuates that figure.
The conservation of oil will cost a great deal of money. Many people will lose jobs and the nation will suffer from increasing unemployment. Many people in Canada think we can escape world difficulties in respect of a petroleum shortage. They feel we will not be affected because we will be able to maintain a balance between exports and imports. Many nations of the world are becoming worried because the United States balance of imports and exports is sagging-and it is the huge United States market upon which our exports depend. Even now, our manufacturing people are finding it very difficult to sell our products to the United States market. The reason the auto pact is not working well for us is that people in the United States have stopped buying cars as a result of the high price of gasoline.
This rigidity of price in the bill is one of its features that makes me doubt its benefits. I think it will perpetuate the Alice in Wonderland approach that things will be fine, everything will work out and we will escape world difficulties in respect of oil prices. This bill is not practical in that sense, and it might help if the minister would indicate, by an amendment or otherwise, how the price of oil will increase or even decrease in the unlikely event that something happens in world markets to cause such a decrease. It would be worth while if the minister would indicate what the government plans in this regard.
We are all aware of the establishment of petrochemical plants, one in Alberta and one at Sarnia. I am sure hon. members are aware of the suggestion that the petrochemical plant at Sarnia would be adversely affected if the Canadian price of oil were equivalent to the world price. Presumably that situation will come about and that plant will find itself in difficulties. Those are the few comments I wanted to make, Mr. Chairman.
